analysis.one_liner: Opens federal coasts and an Alaska refuge to drilling, and suspends federal gas taxes above $3 a gallon.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote in either committee, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lift restrictions on oil and gas leasing across the Outer Continental Shelf and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, revoke presidential drilling withdrawals, and make federal environmental impact statements exempt from lawsuits. On the tax side, it gives refiners 100% expensing and faster depreciation on new refining equipment, and it suspends the federal tax on highway motor fuels any time the national average retail gas price rises above $3.00 per gallon, with the Highway Trust Fund made whole from general federal revenue. It would also raise the business mileage deduction to at least 70 cents per mile and let the President grant normal trade relations to Russia and Kazakhstan.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most, through reopened access to the Arctic refuge, coastal waters, and revoked drilling withdrawals. Refiners gain permanent new tax breaks on refining equipment. Drivers and truckers gain when the roughly 18-cent federal gas tax is suspended during periods when regular gas tops $3 a gallon, though the revenue is backfilled by general taxpayers rather than saved.

how_it_helps.text: Suspends the federal tax on highway motor fuels whenever the weekly national average retail price of regular gasoline exceeds $3.00 per gallon, with floor-stock refunds to dealers when the suspension begins.
Backfills the Highway Trust Fund and related trust funds from general Treasury revenue so road programs lose no money during the suspension.
Raises the optional business mileage deduction to no less than 70 cents per mile, and during any fuel-tax suspension lets medical, moving, and charitable driving be deducted at the business rate.

Lets the President extend normal trade relations to Russia and Kazakhstan, ending the Jackson-Vanik amendment's application to them, which the bill's findings argue would expand access to non-Arab oil supplies.

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers bear the cost whenever the fuel-tax suspension is triggered, since the lost revenue is appropriated out of the general fund rather than saved. The public also bears the loss of protected status for Arctic refuge lands and coastal waters, and the loss of the ability to sue over federal environmental impact statements. The Treasury funds new, permanent tax breaks for refinery construction.

drawbacks.text: Because gas was trading near and above $3.00 a gallon through 2011, the suspension would likely have applied most of the time, amounting to a near-permanent repeal of the federal gas tax with the revenue replaced by borrowed general funds.

The bill repeals the statutory ban on developing oil and gas in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain and revokes all presidential withdrawals of Outer Continental Shelf areas from leasing.

It amends the National Environmental Policy Act to make mandatory federal environmental impact statements exempt from judicial review, eliminating the main legal check citizens and groups have had over major federal energy decisions.
New refinery tax incentives — 100% expensing and 5-year depreciation for petroleum refining property — reduce federal revenue with no direct guarantee of lower prices for consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The driver-facing benefit is real but small and self-financing on paper only: suspending a tax worth roughly 18 cents a gallon while backfilling the trust fund from general revenue simply moves the cost to the deficit. Against that is a sweeping package for the oil sector — opening the Arctic refuge and coastal waters, ending lawsuits over environmental reviews, and permanent refinery tax breaks — that would be difficult to reverse once leases were sold. The bill was structured as an all-or-nothing package rather than targeting the consumer relief alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Natural Resources committees and then to a Natural Resources subcommittee, and neither committee ever reported it or scheduled any action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on March 15, 2011, and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and the Committee on Natural Resources.
No members of either party signed on as cosponsors.

Two days after introduction, the bill was referred to the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and the record shows no further action of any kind through the end of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from enactment because there was none. The oil and gas industry lost a chance at Arctic refuge and coastal leases; public lands and the general treasury were spared the bill's costs, while drivers never saw the fuel-tax relief it promised.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only supporter was its Republican sponsor, and it attracted zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain and all withdrawn Outer Continental Shelf areas to leasing and revoke presidential drilling withdrawals, a major expansion of access to publicly held resources. The public would bear the environmental and land-loss costs while industry gains the acreage.

Refineries would get 100% expensing and 5-year depreciation on refining property, a permanent tax subsidy for building capacity. More refining capacity could modestly help consumers, but the Treasury bears the cost and prices are not guaranteed to fall.
The fuel-tax suspension and the higher 70-cent mileage deduction directly cut fuel-driven operating costs, and the bill's own findings single out truckers as hard hit by fuel prices.
Making environmental impact statements exempt from judicial review would strip away the main tool environmental groups and affected citizens have used to challenge federal energy projects in court.
